course.title: Spanish-Speaking World: Culture & Civilization
course.description: A tour of the cultures that share the Spanish language, from Roman Hispania and Al-Andalus to the novels of Cervantes, the canvases of Velazquez, flamenco, and modern global pop. Topics and structure draw on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. The prose here is original, written for learners, and credits Wikipedia as its reference backbone.

lessons.title: Diagnostic: how much do you already know?

questions.prompt: The Spanish-speaking world is usually described as two great branches. Which pair names them best?
options: Spain in Europe and Hispanic America across the Atlantic
questions.explanation: Spanish is the shared language of Spain and of most of the Americas from Mexico to Argentina, together called the Hispanic or Spanish-speaking world.

questions.prompt: During the Middle Ages, much of the Iberian Peninsula was ruled by Muslim dynasties under the name...
questions.explanation: Al-Andalus was the name for Muslim-ruled Iberia from 711 until the fall of Granada in 1492.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the novel 'Don Quixote'?
questions.explanation: Miguel de Cervantes published the two parts of 'Don Quixote' in 1605 and 1615; it is often called the first modern novel.

questions.prompt: Which dance grew up along the Rio de la Plata, in Buenos Aires and Montevideo?
questions.explanation: Tango emerged in the port neighborhoods of Argentina and Uruguay in the late nineteenth century.

questions.prompt: The festival Dia de los Muertos, honoring the dead with altars and marigolds, is most strongly associated with...
questions.explanation: Dia de los Muertos is a Mexican tradition, observed on the first and second of November and recognized by UNESCO.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many countries have Spanish as an official or national language?
questions.explanation: Spanish is official in around twenty countries, making it one of the most widespread languages in the world.

questions.prompt: Which artist painted the large anti-war mural 'Guernica'?
questions.explanation: Pablo Picasso painted 'Guernica' in 1937 in response to the bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War.

questions.prompt: The colonial empire that spread Spanish across the Americas began in earnest after which 1492 voyage?
questions.explanation: Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, opening the way for later conquests by Cortes and Pizarro.

lessons.title: The Spanish-speaking world: geography and diversity
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'Hispanic' for people and cultures tied to Spain and Spanish America; 'Latino' or 'Latin American' is broader and can include Portuguese-speaking Brazil.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe the two great branches of the Spanish-speaking world and explain why one shared language still covers such a wide range of peoples, climates, and ways of life. You will be able to place the main regions on a mental map and give a sense of scale: how many speakers, how many countries, how much variety. Warm-up: besides Spain, name three countries where Spanish is the main language of daily life, and try to place each on a continent before you read on.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Spanish-speaking world has two great centers of gravity. One is Spain itself, a country in southwestern Europe on the Iberian Peninsula, which it shares with Portugal. The other is Hispanic America, the long sweep of countries from Mexico in the north, through Central America and the Caribbean, down the Andes and across the southern cone to Argentina and Chile. Spanish is an official or national language in around twenty countries and is spoken by roughly five hundred million people as a first language, a figure that places it among the most spoken languages on Earth. Yet a shared language does not mean a single culture. The dry high plateau of central Spain, the tropical coasts of the Caribbean, the Amazon basin, the Patagonian steppe, and the cities of Mexico and Buenos Aires all belong to this world, each with its own foods, music, and daily rhythms. Unity of language sits atop deep regional diversity.

sections.heading: The map in brief
sections.text: Spain is organized into autonomous communities such as Andalusia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country, several of which have their own co-official languages alongside Spanish. Across the Atlantic, Mexico is by far the most populous Spanish-speaking country, home to more Spanish speakers than any other nation. Central America links the two Americas through small countries like Guatemala and Costa Rica, while the Caribbean adds Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Puerto Rico. South America holds the largest Spanish-speaking landmass, from Colombia and Venezuela in the north to Peru and Bolivia in the Andes and on to Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, and Paraguay. Equatorial Guinea in Africa is the one Spanish-speaking country outside Europe and the Americas. Brazil, often lumped in, actually speaks Portuguese, a reminder that Latin America is wider than the Spanish-speaking world.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the peninsula Spain sits on and the country it shares it with. 2) Which Spanish-speaking country has the most speakers? 3) Name two Spanish-speaking Caribbean nations. 4) Is Brazil part of the Spanish-speaking world? 5) Name the one Spanish-speaking country in Africa. Answers: 1) The Iberian Peninsula, shared with Portugal. 2) Mexico. 3) Any two of Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Puerto Rico. 4) No, Brazil speaks Portuguese. 5) Equatorial Guinea.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming everyone in Spain speaks only Spanish. Several regions also use co-official languages such as Catalan, Galician, and Basque. Mistake: treating 'Latin America' and 'the Spanish-speaking world' as identical; Latin America includes Portuguese-speaking Brazil and French-speaking areas, so the two overlap but are not the same. Exit ticket: (a) About how many countries use Spanish as an official language? (b) Which large American country is Latin American but not Spanish-speaking? Answers: around twenty; Brazil.

lessons.title: A short history: Hispania, Al-Andalus, empire, independence
lessons.grammar_note: 'Reconquista' is the traditional name for the long Christian reconquest of Iberia; historians debate the term, but it remains the standard label for the period ending in 1492.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to sketch the long arc of history behind the Spanish-speaking world in four big movements: Roman Hispania, Muslim Al-Andalus and the Christian Reconquista, the overseas empire, and the independence of the American republics. You will be able to put rough dates on each and explain how each left a lasting mark on language, religion, and culture. Warm-up: which ancient empire do you think gave Spanish most of its vocabulary and grammar, and why?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The story begins with Rome. From the late third century before our era, the Roman Republic and then the Empire conquered the Iberian Peninsula, which they called Hispania. Centuries of Roman rule planted Latin, Roman law, and later Christianity, and it is from spoken Latin that Spanish itself would grow. After Rome weakened, Germanic Visigoths ruled for a time. Then, beginning in 711, Muslim armies crossed from North Africa and conquered most of the peninsula, creating Al-Andalus. For centuries, especially under the Caliphate of Cordoba, this was one of the most advanced societies in Europe, with achievements in science, philosophy, architecture, and agriculture, and a mixed population of Muslims, Christians, and Jews. Christian kingdoms in the north slowly expanded southward in a process later called the Reconquista, which ended in 1492 when Granada, the last Muslim state, fell to the Catholic Monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand.

sections.heading: Empire and independence
sections.text: The year 1492 was doubly decisive, for it was also when Christopher Columbus, sailing for Castile, reached the Caribbean. Over the following decades Spain built a vast overseas empire. Hernan Cortes brought down the Aztec Empire in Mexico between 1519 and 1521, and Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in Peru in the 1530s. The Americas were organized into viceroyalties, and Spanish, along with Catholicism, spread across two continents, mixing with indigenous peoples and languages and with Africans brought by the slave trade. By the early nineteenth century, colonial subjects pushed for self-rule. Between roughly 1808 and 1826, leaders such as Simon Bolivar in the north and Jose de San Martin in the south led wars of independence, while Mexico won its independence in 1821. The empire dissolved into the many separate republics that make up Hispanic America today.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did the Romans call the Iberian Peninsula? 2) In what year did Muslim forces first cross into Iberia? 3) What event in 1492 ended the Reconquista? 4) Who conquered the Aztec and the Inca empires? 5) Roughly when did most Spanish American colonies win independence? Answers: 1) Hispania. 2) The year 711. 3) The fall of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs. 4) Hernan Cortes conquered the Aztecs and Francisco Pizarro the Incas. 5) In the early nineteenth century, mostly between 1808 and 1826.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking Spanish descends from Arabic because of Al-Andalus. Spanish is a Romance language from Latin, though it borrowed many words from Arabic. Mistake: imagining the Reconquista as one continuous war; it was a long, uneven process of many kingdoms over centuries. Exit ticket: (a) From which ancient language did Spanish evolve? (b) Name one leader of Spanish American independence. Answers: Latin; Simon Bolivar or Jose de San Martin.

lessons.title: The Spanish language and its varieties
lessons.grammar_note: 'Castellano' (Castilian) and 'espanol' (Spanish) refer to the same language; the first stresses its origin in the region of Castile, the second its status as a national and world language.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain where Spanish comes from, how many people speak it, and why the Spanish of Madrid, Mexico City, and Buenos Aires can sound so different while remaining one language. You will be able to name a few of the best-known regional differences in pronunciation and grammar. Warm-up: if speakers from Spain, Mexico, and Argentina met, do you think they could understand one another? Make a guess before reading.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Spanish is a Romance language, meaning it descends from the spoken Latin carried across Hispania by the Romans. It took shape in the medieval kingdom of Castile in north-central Spain, which is why it is also called Castilian. Over centuries it absorbed words from Arabic during the era of Al-Andalus, and later from indigenous American languages such as Nahuatl and Quechua, giving everyday terms like chocolate and tomato. Today Spanish has around five hundred million native speakers and many more who use it as a second language, making it the language with the second most native speakers in the world after Mandarin Chinese. Despite that enormous spread, it remains strongly unified: a speaker from Spain and one from Chile can converse with little trouble. Standards are tended by a network of national language academies led by the Royal Spanish Academy, founded in 1713.

sections.heading: Varieties and differences
sections.text: The differences across the Spanish-speaking world are mostly in accent, vocabulary, and a few grammatical habits. In much of Spain, the letters c before e or i and z are pronounced like the English 'th', a feature called distincion, while most of Latin America pronounces them like an 's', called seseo. In Argentina, Uruguay, and parts of Central America, speakers use 'vos' instead of 'tu' for the informal 'you', a pattern known as voseo, with its own verb endings. Vocabulary shifts too: a word for a bus, a car, or a straw can change from country to country. Caribbean Spanish is known for dropping or softening the 's' at the ends of syllables. None of this breaks mutual understanding; it simply gives each region a recognizable flavor, much as English differs between London, Texas, and Australia.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) To what language family does Spanish belong, and from what language did it evolve? 2) What other name is used for Spanish, reflecting its origin? 3) Name one everyday word Spanish took from an indigenous American language. 4) What is 'voseo'? 5) Which body, founded in 1713, helps set standards for the language? Answers: 1) The Romance family, from Latin. 2) Castilian (castellano). 3) Chocolate or tomato. 4) Using 'vos' instead of 'tu' for informal 'you', common in Argentina. 5) The Royal Spanish Academy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing the different accents are separate languages. They are regional varieties of one mutually intelligible language. Mistake: assuming 'Castilian' names a different tongue from 'Spanish'; they are two names for the same language. Exit ticket: (a) Spanish has the second most native speakers after which language? (b) What do we call pronouncing c and z like English 'th', as in much of Spain? Answers: Mandarin Chinese; distincion.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the Spanish-speaking world?
options: One language and one uniform culture
A language shared across Spain and Hispanic America atop deep regional diversity
A group of countries that all speak different languages
questions.explanation: A shared language unites the region while foods, music, and daily life vary widely from country to country.

questions.prompt: Al-Andalus refers to...
options: The Roman name for the peninsula
questions.explanation: Al-Andalus was Muslim-ruled Iberia from 711 to the fall of Granada in 1492, with Cordoba as a famous center.

questions.prompt: Spanish is a Romance language, which means it descends from...
questions.explanation: Spanish evolved from the spoken Latin of Roman Hispania, though it borrowed words from Arabic and other languages.

questions.prompt: The conquest of the Inca Empire in Peru was led by...
questions.explanation: Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in the 1530s; Cortes conquered the Aztecs in Mexico.

questions.prompt: The use of 'vos' instead of 'tu', typical of Argentina, is called...
questions.explanation: Voseo is the use of 'vos' for the informal 'you', with its own set of verb endings.

questions.prompt: Most Spanish American colonies gained independence...
questions.explanation: The wars of independence clustered in the early 1800s, with figures such as Bolivar and San Martin.

lessons.title: Literature: from Cervantes to the Boom
lessons.grammar_note: The Spanish 'Siglo de Oro' (Golden Age) names a period of flourishing roughly from the early sixteenth to the late seventeenth century, not a single hundred-year span.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to name the landmark works and authors of writing in Spanish, from the Golden Age masterpiece 'Don Quixote' to the twentieth-century explosion of Latin American fiction known as the Boom. You will be able to explain why these works matter beyond their own countries. Warm-up: have you heard of a windmill-fighting knight or of a novel where it rains for years and the dead return? Jot down anything you already associate with Spanish-language literature.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The towering figure of Spanish literature is Miguel de Cervantes, whose novel 'Don Quixote' appeared in two parts in 1605 and 1615. It tells of an aging gentleman so steeped in tales of chivalry that he sets out as a knight, mistaking windmills for giants, with his earthy squire Sancho Panza at his side. Funny, sad, and endlessly inventive, it is widely regarded as the first modern novel and one of the greatest books ever written. Cervantes wrote during the Spanish Golden Age, the Siglo de Oro, a period of extraordinary creativity that also produced the prolific playwright Lope de Vega, the dramatist Pedro Calderon de la Barca, and the rival poets Luis de Gongora and Francisco de Quevedo. This was the age when Spanish theater, poetry, and prose reached a brilliance that still shapes the language's literary imagination.

sections.heading: The Latin American Boom
sections.text: Centuries later, writing in Spanish had a second great moment, this time from across the Atlantic. In the 1960s and 1970s a group of Latin American novelists won worldwide attention in what became known as the Boom. Its most celebrated figure was the Colombian Gabriel Garcia Marquez, whose 1967 novel 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' follows the Buendia family through generations in the invented town of Macondo, blending ordinary life with marvels in the style called magical realism. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. Alongside him stood the Peruvian Mario Vargas Llosa, later also a Nobel laureate, the Argentine Julio Cortazar, and the Mexican Carlos Fuentes. Their experiments with time, memory, and the fantastic made Latin American fiction a major force in world literature and introduced magical realism as a lasting contribution.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who wrote 'Don Quixote', and in which two years did its parts appear? 2) What is the name of Don Quixote's squire? 3) What is the Spanish term for the Golden Age? 4) Which novel by Garcia Marquez is set in Macondo? 5) Name the literary style associated with the Boom. Answers: 1) Miguel de Cervantes, in 1605 and 1615. 2) Sancho Panza. 3) Siglo de Oro. 4) 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'. 5) Magical realism.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking 'Don Quixote' is a simple children's adventure; it is a layered, satirical novel that helped invent modern fiction. Mistake: assuming the Boom authors all came from one country. They came from across Latin America, including Colombia, Peru, Argentina, and Mexico. Exit ticket: (a) Which prize did Garcia Marquez win in 1982? (b) Name one other Golden Age writer besides Cervantes. Answers: the Nobel Prize in Literature; Lope de Vega, Calderon de la Barca, Gongora, or Quevedo.

lessons.title: Art: El Greco to Dali
lessons.grammar_note: Painters are often known by one name: 'El Greco' means 'the Greek' and refers to Domenikos Theotokopoulos, who settled in Spain.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to name five painters who define the Spanish tradition and say what each is best known for, spanning more than four centuries from the Renaissance to modern art. You will be able to connect a few famous paintings to their makers. Warm-up: can you already match any of these names to a style or a painting: El Greco, Velazquez, Goya, Picasso, Dali?

sections.heading: The old masters
sections.text: Spanish painting has a line of giants. El Greco, born on the Greek island of Crete around 1541, settled in the city of Toledo and painted intense religious scenes with elongated figures and dramatic light, a style all his own. In the seventeenth century, Diego Velazquez served as court painter to King Philip IV and produced some of the most admired portraits in European art; his masterpiece 'Las Meninas' of 1656 plays a famous game with the viewer's point of view, placing us where the royal couple would stand. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Francisco Goya bridged the old world and the modern. He painted glittering court portraits but also the harrowing 'The Third of May 1808', showing the execution of Spanish civilians, and the brooding, private works known as the Black Paintings. Together these three anchor the classical Spanish tradition.

sections.heading: The modern masters
sections.text: The twentieth century brought two of the most famous artists in the world, both Spanish. Pablo Picasso, born in Malaga in 1881, helped invent Cubism, a way of breaking objects into shifting geometric planes, and worked across painting, sculpture, and print with restless energy. His enormous 1937 mural 'Guernica', painted in stark black, white, and gray, protests the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War and remains one of the most powerful antiwar images ever made. Salvador Dali, born in Figueres in 1904, became the best-known figure of Surrealism, a movement devoted to dreams and the unconscious. His painting 'The Persistence of Memory' of 1931, with its soft, melting watches draped over a dreamlike landscape, is instantly recognizable. Between them, Picasso and Dali carried Spanish art to the center of the modern movement.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Where was El Greco born, and in which Spanish city did he work? 2) Who painted 'Las Meninas', and for which king did he work? 3) Which Goya painting depicts an execution of civilians? 4) Which movement did Picasso help invent, and what is his famous antiwar mural called? 5) Which Dali painting shows melting watches? Answers: 1) On Crete; he worked in Toledo. 2) Diego Velazquez, court painter to Philip IV. 3) 'The Third of May 1808'. 4) Cubism; the mural is 'Guernica'. 5) 'The Persistence of Memory'.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming El Greco was born in Spain; he was Greek, from Crete, which his nickname records. Mistake: lumping Picasso and Dali into one style. Picasso is tied above all to Cubism, Dali to Surrealism. Exit ticket: (a) In what year did Picasso paint 'Guernica', and what event prompted it? (b) Which movement is Dali most associated with? Answers: 1937, the bombing of Guernica in the Spanish Civil War; Surrealism.

lessons.title: Music, dance, and festivals
lessons.grammar_note: Flamenco has three intertwined parts: 'cante' (song), 'toque' (guitar playing), and 'baile' (dance).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to name the signature music and dance of the Spanish-speaking world and say where each comes from, and you will be able to describe three of its most famous festivals. You will be able to connect a sound or a celebration to the right country or region. Warm-up: which of these have you heard of: flamenco, tango, salsa, reggaeton, La Tomatina, Dia de los Muertos? Note what you associate with each.

sections.heading: Music and dance
sections.text: Music runs deep across this world. Flamenco, from the southern Spanish region of Andalusia, weaves together passionate singing, intricate guitar, and stamping dance, with roots in Romani, Andalusian, and other traditions; it is recognized by UNESCO as part of humanity's intangible heritage. Across the Atlantic, the tango grew in the port districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo along the Rio de la Plata in the late nineteenth century, becoming a worldwide symbol of romance and melancholy. Salsa developed in the mid-twentieth century from Afro-Cuban and Puerto Rican rhythms, taking much of its modern shape among Latino communities in New York before spreading everywhere as dance-floor music. More recently, reggaeton emerged from Puerto Rico and Panama in the 1990s and 2000s, built on its distinctive dembow beat, and has become one of the most popular styles in global pop.

sections.heading: Festivals and traditions
sections.text: Festivals bring these cultures into the street. La Tomatina, held in the small town of Bunol near Valencia on the last Wednesday of August, is a massive, good-natured tomato fight in which thousands of people pelt one another with ripe tomatoes. Dia de los Muertos, the Mexican Day of the Dead on the first and second of November, is a warm remembrance of the dead, with home altars, marigold flowers, sugar skulls, and favorite foods set out to welcome departed relatives. Semana Santa, Holy Week before Easter, fills cities across Spain, most famously Seville, with solemn processions of religious brotherhoods carrying elaborate floats. Other great celebrations include the running of the bulls during the San Fermin festival in Pamplona and the fiery Fallas of Valencia. Together they show how religion, history, and sheer joy mix in public life.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) From which Spanish region does flamenco come, and what are its three parts? 2) Along which river did tango develop? 3) Which country is reggaeton most associated with? 4) Where and when is La Tomatina held? 5) In which country is Dia de los Muertos celebrated, and on what dates? Answers: 1) Andalusia; cante, toque, and baile. 2) The Rio de la Plata, in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. 3) Puerto Rico. 4) In Bunol, near Valencia, on the last Wednesday of August. 5) Mexico, on the first and second of November.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking flamenco is just a dance; it equally involves song and guitar. Mistake: imagining Dia de los Muertos is a sad or frightening occasion; it is a loving, often colorful celebration of remembrance, not the same as Halloween. Exit ticket: (a) Which festival features processions of religious brotherhoods, especially in Seville? (b) Name the rhythm at the heart of reggaeton. Answers: Semana Santa (Holy Week); the dembow.

questions.prompt: 'Don Quixote' is widely regarded as...
questions.explanation: Cervantes's 'Don Quixote' is often called the first modern novel for its depth, irony, and realistic characters.

questions.prompt: Diego Velazquez's 1656 masterpiece, painted for the court of Philip IV, is...
questions.explanation: 'Las Meninas' is Velazquez's famous court scene that plays with the viewer's point of view.

questions.prompt: Magical realism, blending the ordinary with the marvelous, is most associated with...
questions.explanation: Garcia Marquez's 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' is the signature work of magical realism.

questions.prompt: Flamenco originated in which region of Spain?
questions.explanation: Flamenco grew up in Andalusia in the south and combines song, guitar, and dance.

questions.prompt: Which festival is a large tomato fight held near Valencia?
questions.explanation: La Tomatina takes place in Bunol on the last Wednesday of August.

questions.prompt: Which modern style emerged from Puerto Rico and Panama in the 1990s and 2000s?
questions.explanation: Reggaeton, built on the dembow beat, arose in Puerto Rico and Panama and became a global pop force.

lessons.title: Food, daily life, religion, and global influence
lessons.grammar_note: 'Tapas' are small plates meant for sharing; 'sobremesa' is the relaxed conversation that lingers at the table after a meal.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe the food and daily rhythms of the Spanish-speaking world, explain the place of religion in its societies, and give examples of how this culture shapes the globe today through film, music, and sport. Warm-up: name one Spanish or Latin American dish you have eaten or heard of, and one Spanish-speaking performer or athlete you can think of.

sections.heading: Food and daily life
sections.text: Food is central to social life. In Spain, people often gather over tapas, small shared plates that turn eating into a sociable evening, and over regional dishes such as paella, a rice dish from Valencia, and cured jamon. Meals tend to come late by northern European standards, and a leisurely sobremesa, the talk that lingers after eating, is prized. Across Latin America the table is just as varied: tacos and mole in Mexico, arepas in Colombia and Venezuela, ceviche along the Pacific coast of Peru, the grilled meats of the Argentine asado, and empanadas almost everywhere. The old idea of a midday siesta, a pause in the hottest hours, is less common in modern working cities than outsiders imagine, but the broader value is real: daily life is built around shared meals, family, and unhurried time together.

sections.heading: Religion, society, and global reach
sections.text: Religion shaped these societies deeply. Roman Catholicism arrived with the empire and became the dominant faith across Spain and Hispanic America, leaving its mark on calendars, festivals like Semana Santa and Dia de los Muertos, and family life. In recent decades Spain has grown markedly more secular, while in parts of Latin America other Christian churches have expanded, so the religious picture is changing. Culturally, the Spanish-speaking world now reaches far beyond its borders. Filmmakers such as Pedro Almodovar in Spain and award-winning Mexican directors have shaped world cinema. Performers singing in Spanish, from Latin pop stars to reggaeton artists, top global charts. Football is a shared passion, with clubs like Real Madrid and Barcelona followed worldwide and players from Argentina among the most celebrated on Earth. Spanish is also one of the fastest-growing languages of study, extending this cultural influence further still.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What are tapas? 2) Which country is paella most associated with within Spain? 3) Name a traditional dish from Peru and one from Argentina. 4) Which faith became dominant across the Spanish-speaking world? 5) Name one way the Spanish-speaking world influences global culture today. Answers: 1) Small shared plates eaten socially. 2) Spain, specifically the Valencia region. 3) Ceviche from Peru and the asado from Argentina. 4) Roman Catholicism. 5) Through cinema, globally popular music, football, or the spread of the language.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing everyone in Spain still takes a daily siesta; in modern cities this is far less common than the stereotype suggests. Mistake: assuming the whole region is uniformly and unchangingly Catholic; Spain has secularized and Latin America's religious landscape is shifting. Exit ticket: (a) What is the 'sobremesa'? (b) Name one globally famous football club from Spain. Answers: the lingering conversation after a meal; Real Madrid or Barcelona.
